title: Photo Cache Ring
story: A photo site keeps thumbnails on a few cache servers. With hash(key) mod N, going from four servers to five moves about 4 in 5 keys, and the flood of cache misses hits the database at once. A hash ring moves only the keys next to the new server's points. Each server sits at several points (virtual nodes) to even out the load, and a key can be stored on the next few distinct servers clockwise, so a copy survives when one server dies.
This is the ring from Consistent Hashing, used to spread keys across cache servers (Caching) and to choose replicas in leaderless key-value stores (Design a Key-Value Store).
task: The ring has positions 0 to 232 − 1. Positions come from ringHash(s), a 32-bit FNV-1a hash plus a mixing step, given in the starter code so JavaScript and Python agree exactly. Use it as it is.
• constructor(vnodes) sets the number of points that every server gets, vnodes.
• addNode(name): add the server's points. Point i (0 to vnodes − 1) has the label name + "#" + i and sits at ringHash(label). Adding a server already on the ring does nothing.
• removeNode(name): remove all of that server's points. Removing a server not on the ring does nothing.

• owners(key, count): start at position ringHash(key) and walk clockwise. The first point is the one at or after that position, and the walk then moves to the next point, wrapping from the highest position to the lowest. Collect server names in the order you meet them, skipping servers already collected, until you have count names or have seen every server. Return the list. An empty ring gives [].
If two points share a position, the one whose label sorts first (by character codes) comes first clockwise.
constraints: At most 20 servers on the ring at once; names are 1 to 20 letters, digits or hyphens
Keys are 1 to 40 printable ASCII characters

examples.explanation: In millions, the points are a#0 25.1, a#1 152.6, c#1 414.5, b#0 616.2, b#1 1,845.2 and c#0 3,752.1. "sun.jpg" hashes to 476.3, so the first point is b#0 (cache-b); the second owner skips b#1 (cache-b again) and takes c#0 (cache-c). "photo-3" hashes to 3,939.4, past the last point, so it wraps to a#0, then a#1 (skipped), c#1, b#0. After cache-b leaves, "sun.jpg" moves to c#0 while "photo-3" stays on cache-a: only cache-b's keys moved. With two servers left, asking for 3 owners returns 2.
An empty ring has no owners. Adding "solo" twice still leaves one server, so asking for 2 owners returns one. Removing a server that was never added changes nothing.

hints: Ignore servers for now and think of points on a circle. If the points are sorted, how do you quickly find the first one at or after a position? What if there is none?

Keep every point as (position, label, server) in a list sorted by position, then label. Binary search finds the first point with position ≥ the key's position; if it runs off the end, start at index 0.
For several owners, keep walking from that index, wrapping with % points.length, and skip servers already in a "collected" set. Stop after count servers or one full lap.
Adding a server inserts its vnodes points and keeps the list sorted; removing filters its points out. A set of servers on the ring makes duplicate adds and unknown removes easy to ignore.
bruteForce: For each lookup, compute the clockwise distance from the key to every point, (point − key) mod 232, and sort. This is correct but costs O(P log P) per lookup for P points, which with 20 servers × 50 points means sorting 1,000 points for every cache read.
Servers join or leave rarely, so the points can be sorted once at that time, and each lookup then needs only a binary search and a short walk.

walkthrough: The ring is a sorted list of points. A lookup is a binary search for the first point at or after the key's position, then a clockwise walk that wraps with % n. Servers change rarely, so re-sorting when one is added is acceptable, while lookups happen on every cache read and need to be fast.
Trace the first example (positions in millions). Sorted points: a#0 25.1, a#1 152.6, c#1 414.5, b#0 616.2, b#1 1,845.2, c#0 3,752.1.

• For owners("sun.jpg", 2), the hash is 476.3 and the binary search lands on index 3, which is b#0, so the first owner is cache-b. Index 4 is b#1, which is cache-b again, so it is skipped. Index 5 is c#0, so the second owner is cache-c, and the walk stops with two names.

• For owners("photo-3", 3), the hash 3,939.4 is above every point, so the search returns 6, which equals n, and 6 % 6 = 0 wraps to a#0 (cache-a). The walk then skips a#1, takes c#1 (cache-c), and takes b#0 (cache-b).
• After cache-b is removed, the list is a#0, a#1, c#1, c#0. "sun.jpg" now lands on index 3, which is c#0 (cache-c), and "photo-3" still wraps to cache-a.

Without the skip-seen set, a server's second virtual node would count as a second replica, and both copies of a key would sit on one machine. Stopping once every server is collected keeps the walk to one lap when count exceeds the number of servers.
solution.timeWhy: Per lookup: binary search over P points, then a walk that usually stops after a few points and never goes past one lap. Adding a server re-sorts: O(P log P), rare.
solution.spaceWhy: P = servers × vnodes points, each with its position, label and server.
solution.takeaway: Consistent hashing is a sorted array of points plus a binary search that wraps around. Virtual nodes even out the load, and walking clockwise while skipping servers you already have gives a replica list where each copy is on a different machine.
